## Two ways to count whales

|   | Visual line transects | eDNA |
|---|---|---|
| **What is recorded** | Groups seen, their size and distance from the line | DNA copies in a filtered water sample |
| **What it tells us about density** | Absolute: animals per km², after correcting for detection | Relative: copies depend on shedding, decay and transport |
| **Where it works** | Daylight, calm seas, animals at the surface | Any weather; samples at depth; species that are hard to see |
| **Where it struggles** | Rare or cryptic species, rough seas | Turning copies into animals |

: {.big}

::: {.notes}
~45 s. The audience knows eDNA; the point here is that the two data types fail in different places. Visual surveys give absolute density but are limited by sightability; eDNA sees more but only on a relative scale. Neither on its own gives the full picture, and they fail in complementary ways.
:::

## Project goals

::: {.incremental}
- **One density surface per species**, informed by both data streams at once
- **Calibrate eDNA against animals:** let visual data set the scale that links DNA copies to density
- **Fill gaps:** eDNA where there is little visual effort, or for species rarely seen
- **Honest uncertainty:** each data source keeps its own observation model
- **Test on simulations first**, where the truth is known
:::

::: {.notes}
~45 s. The core idea: treat eDNA and sightings as two noisy, indirect windows onto the same thing, the density of animals in space. A Bayesian state-space model: one latent process, two observation processes. We build and validate it on simulated data before trusting it with real data.
:::

# The data

## Two surveys, one coast

**Visual line transects** (2018 CCES)

- `r km_eff` km of effort in `r n_seg` segments
- Perpendicular distances, group sizes, Beaufort sea state

**eDNA** (2019)

- `r n_bot` water bottles, 0--500 m depth
- **qPCR** for Pacific hake
- **Metabarcoding** (MarVer1) for all vertebrates

**Study area:** north of 35°N, a 690 × 1,770 km box
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~45 s. Two different cruises in two different years. The visual survey covers more ground and goes further offshore; the eDNA stations are concentrated on the shelf and slope, sampled at several depths. Everything in this talk, simulated or real, is on the same study domain north of 35°N.
:::

## Pacific hake: the eDNA anchor

:::: {.columns}

- Not surveyed visually

:::

::: {.notes}
~30 s. Hake is not a marine mammal, but it earns its place in the model. It is in nearly every bottle, has qPCR as well as metabarcoding, and so it tells the model how noisy bottles are and how much non-target DNA there is. Those terms are shared with the whale species, which are near the detection limit.
:::

# The model

## The core idea: one latent field per species

$$
\log \lambda_s(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \underbrace{\mu_s}_{\text{intercept}} \;+\; \underbrace{f_s(X, Y)}_{\text{spatial GP}} \;+\; \underbrace{h_s(Z_\text{bottom})}_{\text{depth spline}}
\qquad \text{animals per km}^2
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="edna">**eDNA**</span>: expected copies in bottle $i$

$$
\mu_{is} = \lambda_s(\mathbf{x}_i)\times c_s \times v_i \times \omega_s(z_i)
$$

conversion factor $c_s$, litres filtered $v_i$, water-column offset $\omega_s$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<span class="vis">**Visual**</span>: expected groups on segment $j$

$$
\mathbb{E}[n_j] = \frac{\lambda_s(\mathbf{x}_j)}{\mathbb{E}[\text{group size}_s]}\times 2L_j \times \text{ESW}_{j}
$$

segment length $L_j$, effective strip half-width $\text{ESW}_j$
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~1 min. This one slide is the whole model. A single log-density surface per species, in animals per km^2, and two observation models hanging off it. On the eDNA side density becomes expected copies through a conversion factor, volume filtered and a water-column offset. On the visual side density becomes expected groups seen through the standard distance-sampling quantities. Same lambda in both.
:::

## The latent field: a Hilbert-space Gaussian process

```{r}
#| out_h: 0.56
fig("hsgp_illustration.png")
```

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Anisotropic GP:** separate length-scales east--west and along the coast
- **HSGP approximation:** the GP is a weighted sum of fixed sine waves (up to 800), so the sampler fits hundreds of weights instead of an $N \times N$ covariance
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Bottom depth:** smooth spline, 4 df
- **Priors from the survey design only:** sample spacing, domain size and basis budget, never the counts
- Fitted in **Stan**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~1 min 15 s. A Gaussian process is a flexible prior over smooth surfaces. The HSGP approximation (Riutort-Mayol et al. 2023) writes it as a weighted sum of fixed basis functions: the sampler only estimates the weights, which makes a coast-wide 2-D surface fast to fit. Ocean structure runs along the coast, so we let the length-scales differ by direction. The priors on the length-scales come only from where we sampled, so the same prior applies to every data source and to real data.
:::

## eDNA observation model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| out_h: 0.84
fig("model_edna.png")
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
- **Bottle copies** $C_{is} \sim \text{NB}(\mu_{is}, \theta)$: bottles vary even at the same density
- **Non-target "junk" DNA** $J_i$, with its own spread $\theta_\text{junk}$
- **qPCR** (hake): detection with probability $1 - e^{-\kappa C}$; Ct falls linearly with $\ln C$
- **Metabarcoding**: reads split among species and junk in proportion to copies; zero-inflated beta-binomial
- Replicates share their bottle's copies
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~1 min 45 s. Read the diagram top to bottom: purple boxes are estimated, coral are latent (one per bottle), teal are observed. Density sets expected copies; the actual copies in a bottle are a negative-binomial draw, so between-bottle noise is not mistaken for spatial structure. qPCR and metabarcoding replicates both look at the same bottle copies. Metabarcoding is compositional, so we model all non-target DNA as a "junk" category that also varies between bottles. Leaving out either noise term biases the field.
:::

## Visual observation model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| out_h: 0.84
fig("model_visual.png")
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
- **Encounters:** groups per segment are Poisson with mean $\lambda / \mathbb{E}[s] \times 2L \times \text{ESW}$
- **Distances:** half-normal or hazard-rate detection, truncated at $w$; $\log\sigma = \log\sigma_0 + \beta_\text{size}(s-\bar s) + \beta_\text{bft}(\text{Bft}-3)$
- **Group size:** modelled, with size-bias correction
- Same field, units and priors as the eDNA side
- $g(0) = 1$ assumed (for now)
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~1 min 15 s. This is a spatial distance-sampling model, fitted in one step. Segment counts carry the spatial signal; perpendicular distances estimate the detection function and so the effective strip width. Larger groups are seen further away, which is corrected for. Beaufort is a covariate on detection, because rough seas are also spatially structured and would otherwise look like low density.
:::

## The joint model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| out_h: 0.84
fig("model_joint.png")
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
- **One field per species** feeds both observation models
- **Switches** turn either likelihood off: eDNA-only, visual-only and joint fits share priors, basis and starting values, and differ only in data
- With one side switched off, it reproduces the single-source model exactly
- **Conversion factors** $c_s$ can be **estimated** for the cetaceans
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~1 min 15 s. Put the two together and you get this: the shared density field in the middle, eDNA on the left, sightings on the right. Because the comparison fits are literally the same model with a likelihood switched off, any difference in performance is due to the data, not to different priors or code. We checked that switching one side off reproduces the single-source models' log density to numerical precision.
:::

## Why combining should help

::: {.incremental}
- **eDNA alone** sees only $\lambda_s \times c_s$, so it can map *relative* density but cannot separate density from the conversion factor
- **Visual data** fix the absolute scale of $\lambda_s$, so the joint model can **estimate $c_s$**: copies per unit of animal density
- **eDNA** adds information where visual effort is thin or sightings are few, sharpening the surface
- **Shared noise terms**, learned mostly from hake, carry over to the rare whale signals
:::

::: {.notes}
~45 s. The key identifiability point for an eDNA audience: in an eDNA-only model, density and the copies-per-animal conversion factor only appear as a product. The visual data break that tie. That gives us an estimate of the conversion factor, which is exactly the quantity eDNA needs to become quantitative, and it comes with uncertainty.
:::

# Simulation study

## Simulation design

| Species | eDNA | Visual detections | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pacific hake | qPCR + metabarcoding | not surveyed | eDNA-rich anchor |
| Humpback whale | metabarcoding | ~800--1,700 | rare in eDNA, conspicuous at the surface |
| Pacific white-sided dolphin | metabarcoding | ~100--150 | weak in both |

: {.big}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Study box north of 35°N, 690 × 1,770 km
- 200 eDNA stations; 35 east--west transects in 10 km segments
- True length-scales: 50 km east--west, 150 km along the coast
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Four fits per dataset: **eDNA-only, visual-only, joint, joint with $c_s$ free**
- Scored on field $R^2$, 95% interval width and coverage, and recovery of $c_s$
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~45 s. One simulated field per species, observed by both survey types. The three species span the range of how informative each source is. Each simulated dataset is fitted four ways with the same model, and we compare how well each recovers the true density surface.
:::

## Results: one simulated dataset, four fits

```{r}
#| out_h: 0.86
fig("results_field.png")
```

::: {.notes}
~1 min. This is one simulated dataset, fitted four ways: the same model with the eDNA likelihood, the visual likelihood or both switched on. Each point is a location, an eDNA station or a transect segment, with the true log density on the x axis and the posterior mean on the y axis. Hake has no visual data, so its joint fit is just its eDNA fit, as it should be. Humpback is carried by the 1,700 sightings; eDNA alone is weak for it. PWSD is weak in both sources alone, R-squared about 0.6 either way, and the joint fit gets to 0.75 with narrower intervals. That is the case the joint model is for.
:::

## Results: what the joint model adds

| Field $R^2$ (CI width) | eDNA only | Visual only | Joint | Joint, $c_s$ free |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hake | 0.94 (2.6) | not surveyed | 0.94 (2.6) | 0.94 (2.6) |
| Humpback | 0.49 (4.2) | 0.92 (1.3) | **0.93 (1.3)** | 0.93 (1.3) |
| PWSD | 0.59 (4.1) | 0.59 (3.2) | **0.75 (2.8)** | 0.74 (2.8) |

: {.big}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **$c_s$ recovered** (log scale): humpback 5.30 [5.05, 5.53], truth 5.30; PWSD 4.77 [4.45, 5.08], truth 4.70
- True field covered: 92--96% in every fit
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Converged: no divergences, $\hat{R} \le 1.06$ (eDNA-only 1.11, bottle noise)
- One dataset so far; replicates running
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~1 min 15 s. The numbers behind the figure. Hake is identical across the eDNA, joint and joint-with-free-conversion fits, which is the sanity check. For humpback the joint fit edges out visual-only. For the dolphin both sources alone are mediocre and together they are clearly better: R-squared from 0.59 to 0.75 and narrower intervals. When we let the conversion factors float, the joint model recovers them: that is the copies-per-animal number eDNA needs to become quantitative, and eDNA alone cannot estimate it. Caveat: this is one simulated dataset; more replicates are running now. Starting values matter: from a flat start the eDNA side can get stuck at extreme hot spots, so the fits start from a field built from the data.
:::

## Next steps

- **Replicates:** more simulated datasets (running now)
- **Real data:** fit the joint model to the 2018 sightings and 2019 eDNA
- **eDNA inputs:** qPCR Ct values and standard curves; volumes filtered
- **Detection:** Beaufort covariate in the joint model's visual side; $g(0)$
- **Different years:** the surveys are a year apart, so the joint fit assumes a stable density surface
- **eDNA transport and decay:** where the DNA is is not quite where the animal is

::: {.notes}
~45 s. The machinery works on simulations; the open problems are mostly about data. The real eDNA data are missing Ct values and filtered volumes, so the absolute conversion factor is not yet meaningful. The two surveys are a year apart. And eDNA moves and decays, which the model treats only through the noise terms for now.
:::
